title: Chapter 33: The Stalk of Grass 1
content:
Chapter 33

Eastern Shu was a labyrinth of sprawling river valleys and jagged, wall-like ridges. The terrain was harsh, the winds were faint and dead, and a heavy mantle of mist choked the valleys for most of the year.

The pair pressed straight on, guided by the severed left hand until they passed a tiny, isolated village.

A patchwork fence of woven brambles boxed in a cluster of mud-walled huts with thatched roofs. Hens and speckled chicks wandered in and out of the dirt yards, pecking at grains of rice. Up on one of the ridgepoles perched a rooster with striking, iridescent feathers; it ruffled its comb, balanced stoically on a single spur, and swept its neck around, surveying its small domain with regal vigilance.

Mercifully, not a single household kept a dog. The locals clearly barely tasted meat all year round, let alone had spare bones to toss to a guard hound.

Just past the perimeter sat a fork splitting into three distinct trails. Two of the paths were worn down to bare earth, peppered with fresh footprints—clearly walked every day. The third, however, was choked with weeds that had long since swallowed the track whole. Tilted at a crooked angle at the mouth of the path was a weathered stone slab. Time and the elements had taken their toll: a hairline crack split the stone clean from crown to base, dry scrub bursting through the fracture.

Two characters were chiseled into the granite, marking the destination. The bottom character was faintly legible asCheng—city. The top, however, was complex, dense with strokes, and cut straight through by the fissure, leaving flecks of chipped rock where the meaning should have been. Wei Wuxian bent down, brushing the weeds aside, squinting at the worn carving for a good while without deciphering a thing.

Naturally, the severed arm’s bearing locked dead onto this exact route.

Wei Wuxian straightened up. "Why don't we ask the locals?"

Lan Wangji dipped his chin. Wei Wuxian obviously didn't expect the man to strike up a chat himself, so he flashed a bright, easy smile and strolled over to a cluster of farm women scattering grain in a nearby yard.

The women—some young, some elder matriarchs—tensed up the second a strange young gentleman approached, looking moments away from tossing their woven baskets and bolting into the huts. But after a few gentle, teasing pleasantries from Wei Wuxian, their guard melted, replaced by shy, blushing replies.

Wei Wuxian pointed back toward the cracked marker with a casual question. Instantly, the color drained from their faces. After a tense beat of hesitation, they began speaking in hushed, halting tones, gesturing vaguely down the weed-choked trail. All the while, not a single one dared steal a glance toward Lan Wangji standing cold and silent by the stone slab.

Wei Wuxian listened with genuine focus, a lazy smirk tugging at the corner of his lips. Before long, he smoothly steered the conversation to lighter waters, coaxing the women into easy, bashful smiles until the stiffness evaporated entirely.

Lan Wangji stood in the distance, watching. After an eternity of waiting with zero sign of the conversation wrapping up, he slowly lowered his gaze to a pebble resting beside his boot.

He nudged the poor, innocent stone with the tip of his sole, rolling it back and forth, grinding it into the dirt for quite some time. When he finally looked back up, Wei Wuxian was pulling something from his breast robes, handing it to the young woman who had done most of the talking.

Lan Wangji froze. He couldn't hold back anymore.

Right as he shifted his weight to march over, Wei Wuxian finally clasped his hands behind his back and came sauntering leisurely back down the lane.

Falling into step beside Lan Wangji, he teased, "Hanguang-jun, you really should've come over. They've even got a hutch of rabbits back in that yard!"

Lan Wangji didn't rise to the bait, offering an icy, flat query instead: "What did you learn?"

"That trail leads to Yi City," Wei Wuxian said. "The top character isYi."

Lan Wangji murmured, "As in righteousness?"

"Yes and no."

"Explain."

Wei Wuxian replied, "The stroke order matches, but the meaning is entirely backwards. It’s not theyiof chivalry—it’s theyiof a mortuary."

They stepped over the brambles and onto the choked path, leaving the weathered marker behind.

Wei Wuxian continued, "The ladies told me that since ancient times, six or seven out of every ten people born in that city meet an early grave—either taken by strange sicknesses or violent deaths. The town is crawling with mortuaries built to house the dead. On top of that, their regional trade is the funeral industry: coffin carpentry, spirit money, and paper effigies. Their craftsmanship is supposedly unrivaled, so the name stuck."

The trail was rough, littered with hidden ruts and jagged stones poking through the brush. Lan Wangji’s eyes stayed glued to the dirt beneath Wei Wuxian's boots, tracking every step.

Wei Wuxian kept up the commentary: "They mentioned folks out here rarely head in, and the locals in the city almost never leave except to haul out funeral shipments. Barely a soul has been spotted on this road in years. It's been abandoned for a good while. Certainly explains why it’s murder on the shins."

"And?" Lan Wangji prompted.

"And what?"

Lan Wangji’s voice was clipped. "What did you give them?"

"Oh. That?" Wei Wuxian chuckled. "Just a tin of rouge."

Back in Qinghe, he’d bought a jar of cheap cosmetics off that quack peddler while asking after Xinglu Ridge, keeping it tucked in his sash ever since. "You can't ask for directions without offering a little courtesy in return. I tried to hand them silver, but it terrified them so much they wouldn't take a coin. They seemed taken with the floral scent—probably never laid hands on cosmetics like that out here—so I gave it away."

Catching the look in the man's eye, Wei Wuxian raised an eyebrow. "What's that stare for, Hanguang-jun? Sure, it wasn't high-end powder. But I'm not like I used to be—I don't walk around with pockets full of fresh blooms, hairpins, and trinkets to toss to every pretty girl I pass. Had nothing else on me. Better than empty hands, right?"

As if an old, deeply irritating memory had been dragged into the light, the corner of Lan Wangji’s brow twitched. He turned his head away in stony silence.

As they pushed deeper, the weeds thinned out, retreating toward the verges as the trail widened. The mist, however, grew suffocatingly dense.

By the time the severed left hand balled its fingers into a tight, resting fist, a crumbling city gate loomed at the end of the road.

The watchtower atop the rampart was missing half its tiles and paint, a whole corner sheared away into jagged ruin. The walls were scarred by erratic, faded graffiti. The red lacquer on the heavy gates had weathered down to an ashen gray, the iron studs black with crusty rust. The double doors hung slightly ajar, as though someone had just pushed a gap through the timber and slipped inside.

Even from the threshold, the place radiated a quiet, rotting wrongness.

Wei Wuxian had spent the hike surveying the landscape. Reaching the gate, he gave his verdict: "Atrocious geomancy."

Lan Wangji gave a slow, somber nod. "Barren peaks, treacherous waters."

Yi City was hemmed in on all sides by sheer cliffs and jagged crags, the rock faces leaning aggressively inward like a closing fist, looking ready to collapse at the slightest tremor. Hemmed in by those looming black precipices under the pale haze, the mountains felt more monstrous than any demon. Standing beneath them pressed down on the lungs, an inescapable, suffocating malice prickling the skin.

Folks always waxed poetic about how remarkable lands nurtured remarkable souls, but the inverse held just as true. Certain geographical cradles were cursed from the roots up—smothered in stagnant, rotten feng shui that doomed their inhabitants to short lives, tragic accidents, and perpetual misfortune. Families rooted there for generations carried that blight straight into their marrow. Malicious anomalies, sudden reanimations, and vengeful wraiths were ten times more common here than anywhere else. Yi City was a textbook case.

Places like this were usually too remote for the great sects to bother with. Frankly, none of them wanted the headache. It was far messier than dealing with a waterborne abyss—you could drive a creature away, but you couldn't rewrite the earth's geomancy. Unless commoners showed up wailing on their doorsteps, the clans simply turned a blind eye and pretended the place didn't exist.

Uprooting and leaving was the only way out, but for families tied to their ancestral dirt, tearing up roots was nearly impossible. Even if six or seven out of ten died young, folks always gambled on being part of the lucky few. So they endured.

Reaching the threshold, the two traded a silent glance.

With a long, grinding squeal of agonizing iron, the unaligned gates groaned open.

Ahead lay no bustling thoroughfares, no charging corpses. Just an endless, suffocating sea of white.

The fog was staggering—easily three times thicker than the mist outside the walls. You could barely make out the straight line of a wide avenue flanked by the dark silhouettes of shuttered buildings, utterly devoid of life.

Instinctively closing the distance between them, they stepped past the gates together.

It was broad daylight, yet the city lay completely dead. No voices, no clatter, not even the distant crow of a rooster or the yip of a dog.

Then again, being the exact spot chosen by that severed arm, it would be far stranger if it weren't cursed.

They pressed down the main street. The deeper they wandered into the belly of the city, the heavier the white shroud fell, smelling faintly of sulfur and rot. At first, they could manage ten paces of visibility; soon, five paces was a blur, until finally, they could barely see their own fingers. The two drifted closer and closer until their shoulders brushed, relying on touch to keep track of each other.

A weird thought crossed Wei Wuxian’s mind:If someone slipped through this mist right between us, turning two into three, would we even notice?

Right then, his boot struck something solid.

Looking down, he couldn't make out the shape through the gloom. Wei Wuxian snagged Lan Wangji’s sleeve to keep him anchored, then squatted down, squinting into the dirt.

A pair of wide, unblinking eyes burst through the fog, staring straight into his face.

It was the severed head of a man—heavy brows, glaring pupils, flanked by two unnervingly bright splotches of round red rouge across his cheeks.

Wei Wuxian had nearly kicked it across the street earlier, so he knew how light it had felt. A real skull wasn't weightless. Reaching out to give the cheek a squeeze, the papery flesh caved right in, smearing cheap red powder onto his fingers.

A paper funeral effigy.

The craft was strikingly lifelike—the makeup was garish, but the underlying facial structure was remarkably delicate. Given the town's trade, their papercraft had to be elite. Mortuary effigies came in all flavors: substitute dolls burned to endure the tortures of the underworld in place of the departed, taking the brunt of boiling oil and mountain-blades; or maidservants sent to knead backs and pour wine in the yellow springs. Pure placebo comfort for the living, of course.

This particular head belonged to a "Shadow Enforcer."

True to the name, they were spiritual bouncers, burned so the dead wouldn't get pushed around by spiteful ghouls or greedy underworld magistrates, ensuring their paper money didn't get mugged in the dark. It must have had a tall, sturdy bamboo-and-paper frame to match, ripped away and tossed into the gutters by god-knows-who.

The hair was styled into a sleek topknot, remarkably glossy. Wei Wuxian ran his thumb along the scalp; the strands were glued down so cleanly they looked like they’d sprouted from the paper skin.

"Impressive work," he muttered. "Real human hair, maybe?"

Out of nowhere, a spindly black shadow brushed right past his ribs!

It moved with uncanny, unnatural speed, grazing his robes before melting straight back into the blinding mist. Bichen cleared its scabbard on instinct, slicing through the air after the blur, only to snap right back into its scabbard with a clean metallic ring.

The thing had moved too fast—far beyond anything mortal legs could manage.

Lan Wangji’s hand rested against his hilt. "Stay sharp."

Brushing shoulders was one thing; next time, it might not be so polite.

Wei Wuxian stood up, brushing off his knees. "Did you catch that sound?"

Lan Wangji replied, "Footsteps. And bamboo."

Right. In that split second, layered beneath the frantic patter of bare soles, a bizarre tapping had echoed across the pavers—a crisp, rapidclack-clack-clack, like a bamboo pole striking stone at high speed. What kind of creature moved like that was anyone's guess.

Before they could ponder it, another wave of footsteps drifted through the whiteout ahead.

This time, the steps were light, halting, and layered—a whole group picking their way forward with extreme caution, moving in dead silence. Flipping his wrist, Wei Wuxian produced an Incinerating Ward, flicking the paper lightly into the murk. If whatever was creeping toward them reeked of malice, the talisman would ignite, buying them light and a clean target.

The party ahead caught the movement of the projectile and countered instantly!

Half a dozen streaks of multicolored sword-glare whistled through the mist, bristling with frantic killing intent!

Bichen cleared its sheath with fluid grace, circling a protective perimeter before Wei Wuxian's chest. With a concussive chime of clashing steel, it swatted the flying swords right back into the fog. Shouts of panic and stumbling boots echoed through the haze.

Recognizing the voices, Lan Wangji recalled Bichen immediately.

Wei Wuxian called out, "Jin Ling?! Sizhui!"

Sure enough, Jin Ling's sharp, incredulous voice tore through the fog: "Why is it always you?!"

"I could ask you the exact same thing!" Wei Wuxian fired back.

Lan Sizhui’s reply came in a breathless rush, barely containing his relief: "Young Master Mo? You're here?! Does that mean Hanguang-jun is with you?!"

Hearing Lan Wangji might be within arm's reach, Jin Ling clamped his mouth shut on instinct, looking for all the world like he’d been hit with a fresh Silence Spell, terrified of catching a scolding.

Lan Jingyi yelled through the gloom, "He has to be! That was Bichen! That was definitely Bichen, wasn't it?!"

"Yeah, he's here," Wei Wuxian called out, amusement lacing his voice. "Standing right beside me. Over here, hurry up."

Realizing they were among allies, the juniors let out a collective sigh of sweet relief, swarming through the fog like ducklings finding their mother. Alongside Jin Ling and the Lan disciples were seven or eight unfamiliar boys in lavish clan robes—lingering traces of panic on their faces, clearly well-bred scions of prominent families.

Wei Wuxian folded his arms. "What are you all doing holed up in a place like this? Throwing lethal strikes the second someone moves—if Hanguang-jun hadn't parried that, what if you hit an innocent civilian?"

Jin Ling snapped back, "There are no innocent civilians out here! There isn't a single living soul in this entire damn city!"

Lan Sizhui nodded solemnly. "It's true. Broad daylight, smothered in demonic fog, and not a single storefront is open."

"We'll get to that," Wei Wuxian said, waving a hand. "First: how did you lot end up together? Don't tell me you agreed to a friendly joint night-hunt."

With Jin Ling's prickly, spoiled temper—picking fights with everyone in his path, not to mention his recent scuffles with the Lan kids—the idea of them holding hands on an expedition was a comedy sketch.

Lan Sizhui, ever polite, stepped forward to explain: "It's a long story. We were originally..."

Right then, a sharp, rhythmicclack-clack-clackpierced the suffocating mist—the frantic, piercing rap of a bamboo cane striking stone, drawing closer by the second.

Every junior's face blanched at once: "It's back!"
